analysis.one_liner: Imposes a tax of 1% to 5% on the price of single-family homes bought by investors who own many homes, and sends the money to affordable-housing funds.
analysis.headline: Ten Democratic senators introduced the bill in January 2026, but the Senate Finance Committee has taken no action on it since it was referred there the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new federal tax on companies and individuals that buy single-family homes while already owning large numbers of them: 1% of the purchase price for investors owning 16 to 25 homes, 3% for those owning 26 to 100, and 5% for those owning more than 100. Small owners, ordinary families buying their own homes, nonprofits, states, public housing authorities, land banks, and community land trusts are exempt, and homes newly built by the buyer don't count. The money raised goes 65% to the federal Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, which finance affordable housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families trying to buy their first home, who would face less competition from large investors bidding up prices on existing houses. Renters and low-income households would benefit from the added funding for affordable housing construction through the Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund. Residents of small states would gain from a new funding formula that replaces a flat minimum with a proportional share.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to investors who already own more than 15 single-family homes, with rates rising from 1% to 5% as their holdings grow, aiming to make it more expensive for large investors to outbid families for existing houses.
Sixty-five percent of the revenue goes to the Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, both of which finance affordable housing construction and preservation.
The bill counts homes owned indirectly through related companies and family members, making it harder for large investors to stay under the ownership thresholds by splitting up their portfolios.
It replaces a flat $3 million small-state minimum in the Housing Trust Fund with a proportional share, which directs more money to smaller states.

analysis.who_pays: Large single-family landlords and investment firms that buy existing homes, who would pay a 1% to 5% tax on each purchase. Some of the cost could be passed through in the form of lower prices offered to sellers or higher rents if investors shrink the rental supply.

drawbacks.text: The tax may not be enough to change behavior: a 1% tax on investors owning 16 to 25 homes is modest, and large investors could absorb a 5% cost or shift toward build-to-rent new construction, which the bill exempts from the tax.

If taxed investors buy fewer homes but also build or keep fewer rentals, some renters could face higher rents or fewer available rental houses in markets where large landlords supply most single-family rentals.
The threshold exempts any investor owning 15 or fewer homes, so the smallest investor-landlords would pay nothing even while competing with first-time buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary buyers, the upside is potentially meaningful in markets where institutional investors are active bidders, and the housing-fund revenue is a direct add-on. The main risk is that the tax is small enough to be absorbed by the largest players and that exempting new construction simply steers investor money toward build-to-rent rather than reducing investor ownership overall. The bill does nothing to force sales of existing investor-owned homes; it only taxes future purchases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee has not scheduled any action on it so far this Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on January 30, 2026, joined by nine Democratic senators as cosponsors and original sponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where tax legislation is considered; the sponsor's remarks appeared in the Congressional Record.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investors in single-family rentals are better off so far, since no purchase tax has advanced; affordable-housing advocates and homebuyers have gained nothing yet but the bill is still alive on paper.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island, bill sponsor

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill a full slate of Democratic Senate support from day one.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has not scheduled a markup, vote, or any further action.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican senator has signed on; the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: Companies owning more than 100 homes would pay 5% of the price of every existing home they buy, directly targeting the business model of buying houses to rent. Their gain comes at the cost of higher purchase prices for ordinary buyers, so the bill's effect runs against the public's interest in affordable ownership.

Landlords owning 16 to 25 homes would pay a 1% purchase tax, and those with 26 to 100 homes would pay 3%. Many are small businesses rather than institutions, though in hot markets they compete with families for the same houses.

Newly built homes are exempt from the ownership count and the purchase tax, so investor demand that shifts from existing houses to build-to-rent construction flows to builders. This exemption is intended to push capital toward adding housing supply rather than bidding up existing stock.

industries.industry: Nonprofit and public affordable housing (community land trusts, land banks, housing authorities)
industries.note: These organizations are exempt from the tax, and 100% of the revenue raised goes to the Housing Trust Fund and the Capital Magnet Fund, which fund affordable housing.

analysis.trajectory: Standalone tax bills introduced in the minority party's name rarely reach the floor, and the Finance Committee has shown no activity on this one. Unless the committee schedules a markup or the bill is folded into a larger tax package, it will likely sit without action for the rest of the Congress, as similar investor-purchase-tax proposals in previous Congresses have.
